common_name: Cascade Hops (Iconic Citrus-Floral American Aroma Hop)

planting.note: Plant rhizome cuttings horizontally 2-3 inches deep in spring in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Cascade climbs vigorously and needs a strong trellis or arbor at least 12-15 feet tall. Only female plants produce usable cones.

directions: Plant rhizomes horizontally in moist, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; provide a tall, sturdy support for the vigorous climbing bine. Cascade, released by Oregon State University in 1972, is the single most influential American hop cultivar, prized for its distinctive grapefruit-citrus and floral aroma that came to define the American craft beer movement and remains the signature hop of classic West Coast pale ales and IPAs. The vigorous vine dies to the ground each fall and re-emerges rapidly each spring to climb 15-20 feet on strings or a trellis; soft green cones ripen in late summer and should be harvested when papery, fragrant, and slightly sticky with lupulin, then dried promptly for brewing. Performs best in cool-summer climates with long day length; struggles with the persistent heat and humidity of zone 8-9 Gulf South summers, so give it the coolest, best-ventilated site available and expect reduced cone yield compared with Pacific Northwest production.
sources: Oregon State University Extension — Hop Cultivar Notes

common_name: Centennial Hops (Super Cascade, Balanced Citrus-Floral Hop)

planting.note: Plant rhizome cuttings horizontally 2-3 inches deep in spring in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Centennial climbs vigorously and needs a strong trellis or arbor at least 12-15 feet tall. Only female plants produce usable cones.

directions: Plant rhizomes horizontally in moist, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; provide a tall, sturdy support for the vigorous climbing bine. Centennial is a Washington State-bred hop, often nicknamed 'Super Cascade' for its higher alpha acid content and similar but more intense citrus and floral aroma compared with Cascade, making it a versatile dual-purpose hop used for both bittering and aroma in American pale ales and IPAs. The vigorous vine dies to the ground each fall and re-emerges rapidly each spring to climb 15-20 feet; cones ripen in late summer and should be harvested when papery, fragrant, and sticky with lupulin resin, then dried promptly. Like other Humulus lupulus cultivars, it performs best in cool-summer, long-day climates and struggles with Gulf South heat and humidity, so plant in the coolest, most open-air site available and expect a smaller harvest than in traditional hop-growing regions.
sources: Washington State University — Hop Variety Notes

Chinook, released by the USDA in 1985, is a high-alpha dual-purpose hop valued for strong bittering power paired with a distinctive piney, spicy, slightly grapefruit aroma, widely used in American IPAs and pale ales that call for assertive hop character. The vigorous vine dies to the ground each fall and re-emerges each spring to climb 15-20 feet on a trellis; cones ripen in late summer and should be harvested when papery, aromatic, and sticky with lupulin, then dried promptly for brewing. Like other hop cultivars, it performs best in cool-summer, long-day climates and struggles with Gulf South heat and humidity, so plant in the coolest, most open-air site available and expect reduced yield compared with traditional hop-growing regions.
sources: USDA Agricultural Research Service — Hop Cultivar Release Notes

Willamette, named for Oregon's Willamette Valley where it is extensively grown, is a widely planted English-type aroma hop bred as a Fuggle-derivative, valued for its mild, pleasant, slightly floral and spicy character well suited to English-style ales, brown ales, and other beer styles calling for a gentler hop presence than the assertive citrus hops popular in American IPAs. The vigorous vine dies to the ground each fall and re-emerges each spring to climb 15-20 feet; cones ripen in late summer and should be harvested when papery, fragrant, and sticky with lupulin, then dried promptly for brewing. Like other hop cultivars, it performs best in cool-summer, long-day climates and struggles with Gulf South heat and humidity, so plant in the coolest, most open-air site available and expect a lighter harvest than in the Pacific Northwest.
sources: Oregon State University Extension — Hop Cultivar Notes

Nugget, released by the USDA in 1982, is a reliable high-alpha American hop grown chiefly for its strong bittering power and productive, vigorous growth, with a robust herbal, slightly piney aroma that makes it a workhorse bittering hop in many American beer styles. It is valued by home growers in part for being an especially heavy yielder and easy to grow compared with some finicky aroma cultivars. The vigorous vine dies to the ground each fall and re-emerges each spring to climb 15-20 feet; cones ripen in late summer and should be harvested when papery, aromatic, and sticky with lupulin, then dried promptly for brewing. Like other hop cultivars, it performs best in cool-summer, long-day climates and struggles with Gulf South heat and humidity.
